hints.hint: In "I don't know" puzzles, never open one case per reading of the public number and ask whether it is consistent overall. Readings usually are, so that test gives no discriminator and you fall back on looks. Sieve private values instead. Each option the problem leaves open, such as which quantity was published, contributes at most one candidate partner to a value v, so v pooled list is short: build it once across all options, keep only legal entries, and allow the two private values to be equal. Stage 1: v is ignorant only if you exhibit two distinct partners; gather those v into K, since the announcement deletes exactly the v with one partner. Stage 2: a later speaker value m keeps only partners lying in K, and survives if two remain. Audit: one survivor, report it; none, you silently fixed the published quantity; many, an announcement is unused. Deriving impossible is never evidence.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 rollouts scored 1/8 (exec 149.398). Four burned the 16384-token cap with no box; the four that terminated wrong all boxed 143. New evidence: the incumbent's contrapositive did get echoed (pooled appears up to 27 times, 'two distinct' in 6 rollouts) yet no rollout ever finished a pooled list. Instead the dominant path is a global case split - open sum-reading and product-reading, check each is consistent with both statements, find BOTH are, then declare a winner on looks (one explicitly called 14x143 'unique', another invoked primality 30 times). That whole-reading consistency test is the trap: it never discriminates, so the rollout must guess. So this revision names and bans it up front, notes each unsettled option yields only one partner per v (making the list cheap to finish), and adds a survivor-count audit whose zero branch diagnoses the illegal fixing rather than licensing a guess.

hints.hint: To find where ALL solutions lie, derive one necessary condition, not the solutions. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n take moduli of whole sides: |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n. Never nth-root a ratio; that spawns a branch per solution. Only nth-root the scalar: |z-a| = k|z-b|, k^n = |c|; write |c| as a prime power, divide its exponent by n. Name the shape first: ratio k != 1 a circle, k = 1 a bisector, constant distance sum an ellipse, difference a hyperbola. Square (z = x+iy), collect A(x^2+y^2)+Bx+Cy+D = 0, divide by A, complete the square, r > 0. Matching that shape is your whole check; containment was asked, so necessity closes it.
hints.mutation: predict-the-locus-shape-from-a-conic-classification-table and make that match the only check; move the ratio-form ban upstream into the derivation
hints.subagent_summary: 8/8 correct, so train is saturated (train_i 1.0) and the lever is transfer plus wasted budget. Every rollout had the modulus ratio and the completed-square circle inside its first ~2k chars, then spent 4-8x more tokens on verification the incumbent bans only at the end: all 8 rewrote to ratio form and nth-rooted it into per-solution branches (10-41 exponential expressions each). The worst (6590 tokens, 25 hedges, 12 'mistake', 6 'contradiction') mis-solved a branch, got a point failing its own modulus ratio, then doubted the modulus law itself for ~4k tokens. Three others closed by calling the condition 'necessary and sufficient': right answer, wrong logic that will not transfer. Diagnosis: a terminal ban leaves the checking urge nowhere legal. So the ratio ban moves upstream into the derivation, and the urge is redirected to a free portable check: classify the locus shape from the condition's form before any algebra, then require only that the completed square match it.

hints.hint: Union = summed areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Frame on the covering shape: put the shared point at the origin with its two edges there as axes, so the cover is the wedge x >= 0, y >= 0. A corner spans only the plus side; never center that shape on the point. Settle overlap by arithmetic, not words: write numeric vertices for the other shape S in this frame, then intersect the x-ranges and the y-ranges. Shared span on both axes forces positive overlap, so no "lies outside" verdict survives; containment needs every S vertex nonnegative in both coordinates, so one negative kills it. Compute overlap once as S clipped to the wedge, shoelace it, box that union immediately. Only then argue extremality: if rotating the wedge by its own angle carries each clipped piece to the next, overlap is angle-free and that union maximal. Never scan orientations or tangency.
hints.subagent_summary: 1/8 correct. No rollout ever computed a clipped area: shoelace appears 0 times in all 8. Three failures used the wedge frame yet ruled by prose: two said the cover "lies outside" S (overlap 0, answered summed areas) and one said S lies wholly inside the aligned cover (overlap = area(S)); each cited coordinate ranges that visibly straddle 0 without comparing them. Four hit the 16384 cap: they reached the right clipped value early, then re-litigated rotation (104-196 rotation mentions, 18-38 tangency) and never boxed. The lone winner reached the same value and closed. The incumbent asserts sign facts ("one negative coordinate kills containment") but never asks for numbers, so nothing is executed. This revision demands numeric vertices then an axis-by-axis range intersection, which refutes both the disjoint and the containment verdict from the same table, and orders shoelace-then-box before any angle talk.

hints.hint: A maximum count is an upper bound meeting a matching construction; produce both. Conditions at the used positions are equations there, not an identity in x: never demand P(n+1) - P(n) be constant for all n, and void any "P must be linear" it yields. Bound by partition: a function may repeat; write the target at index n as T(n), group indices by function used. On P's group, P - T vanishes but is not identically zero, since low-degree T cannot cancel P's leading term: at most d = deg P per group. Sum the caps: N x d, never N; expect far above N. Certify by substitution: give each function a block n_1..n_d, set P = T + c(x-n_1)...(x-n_d), c nonzero; each n_j kills the factor, so P = T there, degree still d.
hints.subagent_summary: 8/8 correct with the incumbent, so aggregation is sound; the cost is one shared detour. All 8 rollouts built a difference operator on the board (P(n+1)-P(n) or P(x+1)-P(x)), demanded it be constant for ALL n, got a degree d-1 polynomial, and concluded "must be linear/constant" - 98 hits total, up to 37 in one rollout - then had to recover. Six also called the product "too large" (18 hits) and reopened tightness. Spend was 8.0k-15.3k tokens with 207 "Wait" restarts; earlier rounds show these loops truncate when they start sooner. The incumbent only bans chaining adjacent terms, justified by "neighbours may differ", which round 19 found is misparsed as "each term needs a distinct polynomial". This revision instead names the real logical error - promoting finitely many point conditions to an identity in x - voids the "must be linear" conclusion outright, and keeps the per-group cap, the sum, and the substitution certificate.

hints.hint: Fit the unknown curve parameters from the given points, then re-check both numerically. A vector equality is ONE constraint, a parallelogram: read the displacement (dx,dy) off it; never add a midpoint or vertex-sum equation, which merely restates it. Carry one unknown vertex (t, f(t)); closure is f(t+dx) = f(t) + dy. BEFORE cross-multiplying, test that closure as decimals at a given vertex's t, which already realizes (dx,dy). Disagreement means you mis-simplified the shifted argument, or inverted the factor dy contributes; it never means the problem is inconsistent. So that t must be a root of the resulting polynomial: divide it out and the rest is easy. No real root, or only given roots, is the same signal. Verify each new coordinate forward (base^y reproduces its argument), then area = |cross product| of adjacent edges.
hints.subagent_summary: 6/8 correct (149.402); both failures hit the 16384-token cap on the SAME stage, forming the closure equation, and never reached the incumbent's root test. One slipped arithmetic inside the shifted argument (wrote t-4/3+1 as t+1/3), so its quadratic had irrational roots and the given vertex was not a root; it never tested that, and spent the rest of the budget on diagonal-midpoint restatements (15 mentions). The other inverted the factor by treating log_{1/2}A+1 as log_{1/2}(2A), got discriminant -92, then declared the problem impossible (8 'no real' passages, 15 midpoint mentions). Its earlier attempt produced a polynomial whose ONLY roots were the two given vertices, another detectable-equation bug. So the revision moves validation upstream: check the closure numerically at a given vertex before any algebra, and route failure to the shift or the factor, not to the problem.

hints.hint:
Convert the asked event into a constraint on the order of moves, never into a symmetry claim: reachable outcomes are unequally likely, so 1/n and 1/n! are wrong here.

Before any arithmetic, write one translation line. Each item placed on a pile sits above what is already there, so bottom = first arrival, k-th from bottom = k-th arrival, top = last arrival. If you find yourself asking which item moves last while the question named the bottom, you have flipped it.

Then list the deciding moves in order and mark each one: forced, only one move legal, weight 1; or genuinely free, two moves legal, weight 1/2. Clearing the items lying above a target costs one free step each, so expect a run of halves. Multiply along the list, then add over the lists satisfying the event.
hints.subagent_summary: 0/8. Part b is the graded quantity and all 8 missed it. Seven (idx 0-5,7) explicitly wrote that the shed's bottom bag is the one carried LAST, then answered 1/4 by symmetry: 'each bag equally likely to move last' or 3!/4! over random permutations. Idx 6 declared the order always reversed (1, 0). Part a was template-guessed: 1/2^(n-1) (idx 0,1,2,5), 1/24 (idx 4,7), 1/256 (idx 3). Not one rollout wrote a concrete move order with per-step legality, so the incumbent's forced/free pricing never gets executed. The incumbent states arrival-rank orientation declaratively and loses to the flip every round. This revision makes the position-to-arrival-time translation a required written line with an explicit self-catch test, and trims length back toward the 91-token variant that holds the best held-out so far, since every rewrite at 175-192 tokens scored held-out 0.2 or worse.

hints.hint:
Huge stated size, one entry asked: the first thing you write must be the smallest numeric version of the same question. Match counts: n unknowns, n conditions, index range 1..n, the nonzero right-hand side last.
Solve n=2,3,4 in exact fractions, showing the elimination. A value counts only if its arithmetic is written out; asserted or remembered small-case answers are inadmissible, and fitting a law to them is how these attempts fail. Cheap route: subtract each condition from the next to kill an unknown, repeat, work back.
Only with three shown cases, read the law from ratios of consecutive values: the ratio names growth -- factorial, binomial, power -- and the sign. A computed case outranks any formula; on a clash, redo that case.
Never expand a product at the stated size or carry that size as a symbol. Substitute it once and stop.
hints.mutation: require-displayed-elimination-per-toy+first-thing-on-page-ordering-gate (asserted/recalled toy values are inadmissible; no general-size algebra until three exact solutions are shown)
hints.subagent_summary: 0/8; 6 hit the 16384 cap. Root cause is new: not one rollout ever solved a small case. Six wrote zero small systems and went straight to full-size symbolic work (48-142 'coefficient of x' mentions, 51-80 of 2004!, Vandermonde/elementary-symmetric detours) and never emitted an answer. The two that terminated only *asserted* toy answers with no arithmetic shown -- one claimed n=3,4 give 1/2 and 1/3 and shipped 1/(n-1); the other claimed -1, 1/2, -1/4 and shipped a power-of-2 law. So the incumbent's ladder is skipped or faked, and its bans on stated-size algebra are ignored because nothing competes for the first line. This revision makes the smallest numeric case the mandatory first thing written, makes a toy value admissible only with its elimination displayed, gates law-fitting behind three displayed solutions, and keeps the proven consecutive-ratio law.

hints.hint: Let N be the unstated count of identical units; recover it from integrality, not from the story. Set up algebra before interpreting: give each listed figure its own per-unit unknown and write figure = N x unknown. A figure under a whole-collection heading is an aggregate, so its unknown is what must be whole; then N divides each figure and admissible N are their common divisors. Select deliberately: if the text bounds the count (a range, at least, at most, roughly), keep only divisors inside that window; otherwise take the maximum feasible count, their gcd. When the story counts groups (streets, rows, batches), write N = groups x units-per-group and solve for the second factor; a group count is never N by itself, even if every total divides by it. Finally sum the per-unit shares, apply any markup as one factor, check each share is whole, and answer what was asked.
hints.subagent_summary: 7/8 public rollouts scored 1 (train_i 0.875). The single failure never doubted the gcd machinery; it mis-assigned roles, reading each listed village-wide figure as a per-house cost. That made total = 525*N with total already 525, so N collapsed to 1, the integrality condition did no work, and it answered a bare cost*1.2. It burned most of 8242 tokens cycling per-house/per-street readings and calling each a contradiction. The incumbent's only defence is 'decide once whether each figure is a grand total or a per-unit amount', which tells the student to stop revisiting but not how to pick. Prior negative screens against bad readings (self-refutation, well-posedness, role-locking) all lost held-out ground, whereas the kept rounds added constructive machinery. So I swapped the passive clause for a constructive setup: name a per-unit unknown per figure and write figure = N x unknown, which fixes aggregates as aggregates by construction and makes integrality bind on the unknowns.

hints.hint: For p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with p,q of equal degree n, skip the degree-n^2 coefficient system. Find a common fixed point r and set p=r+A(x-r)^n, q=r+B(x-r)^n. Composing forces AB^n=BA^n; factor as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 and carry both branches, since B=A means p=q; let the data kill one. An automatic identity is not underdetermination; count free parameters against given conditions. Combine conditions symmetrically: two differing only in the sign of one part add to pin one unknown, subtract to pin the other. Verify p(r)=q(r)=r and evaluate centered. If no centered form fits, do not expand: up to one affine substitution, commuting polynomials are power maps, Chebyshev polynomials, or iterates of a single map - test those.
hints.subagent_summary: 7/8 correct (3.5k-5.4k tokens). The one failure hit the 16384-token cap. It centered correctly, then mis-nested the composition (re-cubing an already-cubed offset: BA^9, so B^2=A^8, B=+-A^4, 16 mentions; 120 r^3 mentions). Both corrupted branches gave high-degree equations in the center, and it spent most of its budget trial-substituting integer centers (2,3,4,5,6,-2,-3,30), then fell back to generic coefficient matching and died in a degenerate repeated-subtraction loop. All 7 correct rollouts reached A^3=B^3 on their first page and closed in one line. Rounds 9/10 (exponent audits), 14/15 (factoring), 16 (no-ratio), 17 (validate-vs-p=q), 18 (conjugation) and 19 (elimination order) all added corrective wording about that same slip and all lost heldout. So this revision leaves the proven spine intact and adds a positive escape hatch instead: name the classification of commuting polynomial families, giving a concrete next move when the centered form does not fit.

hints.hint: For "how many repeats restore the original" problems, decide everything from written states; use no cycle or permutation notation, the usual source of a false order 2. One repeat = ALL listed sub-steps in order, each acting on what the previous produced. When a sub-step swaps a block with the next block of equal length L: slot j trades with slot j+L, so all 2L slots move, each block keeps its internal order, other slots are copied verbatim; never swap within a block. Refute order 2 concretely: write the state after two complete repeats; if it differs from the original, order 2 is dead however self-inverse the sub-steps look. Keep applying complete repeats, writing each state and counting only completed ones, until it first equals the original. Do the two smallest sizes plus one larger; counts must grow and each divide the next, else redo the larger trace.
hints.mutation: states-only, ban cycle/permutation notation; explicit j<->j+L block-swap rule with no intra-block swap; two-repeat order-2 refutation; count only completed repeats; grow-and-divide cross-size filter
hints.subagent_summary: 6/8 wrong. idx1, idx6, idx7 never wrote a state: each sub-step became a transposition, the composite was called disjoint transpositions or an involution, and they boxed 2. idx7 also placed the blocks wrong, writing the length-2 block swap as (1 2)(3 4) - swapping inside a block, not block-to-block - manufacturing the disjointness. idx5 invented per-size cycle lists (6-cycle plus 2-cycle, then an 8-cycle), got 2,4,6,8, boxed 2n. idx4 fabricated 2,4,10,30 and fit a product of primes. idx2 had a correct small-size state trace, then built a permutation table giving order 2 and burned all 16k tokens arguing table versus states. Both correct rollouts just simulated whole repeats on lettered words. The incumbent invites the lcm-of-cycle-lengths cross-check that caused three failures, so the revision bans cycle notation, gives the exact j to j+L block rule with no intra-block swap, a two-repeat order-2 refutation, and a grow-and-divide filter.
